manuscript_metadata.title: Efficacy of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy on Pain Acceptance and Psychological Inflexibility in Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain: A Randomized Controlled Trial

cover_letter_content.hook: Chronic musculoskeletal pain remains one of the primary contributors to global disability, frequently exacerbated by experiential avoidance and behavioral inflexibility. Although pharmacological treatments offer palliative relief, psychological flexibility training has emerged as a transformative paradigm for functional restoration.
cover_letter_content.key_findings: In this randomized controlled trial of 60 chronic pain patients, 8 weekly sessions of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy produced significant reductions in pain-related disability (ηp² = 0.34, p < .001) and psychological inflexibility (ηp² = 0.42, p < .001) compared to treatment-as-usual controls, with treatment gains fully sustained at 3-month follow-up.
cover_letter_content.novelty_statement: To our knowledge, this is the first randomized investigation in the region to examine cognitive defusion and committed action as concurrent longitudinal mediators of pain acceptance trajectories using bootstrap confidence intervals.
cover_letter_content.fit_with_journal: Given the Journal of Contextual Behavioral Science's preeminent reputation in contextual behavioral science and functional contextualist clinical interventions, we believe this manuscript will be of immediate interest to your international readership.

highlights: ACT significantly reduced pain disability in chronic pain patients (p < .001).
Psychological inflexibility was reduced with a large effect size (ηp² = .42).
Gains in pain acceptance were fully sustained at 3-month follow-up.
Cognitive defusion significantly mediated treatment outcomes over time.

revision_rebuttal.introductory_letter: We thank the Editor and the two anonymous reviewers for their thoughtful, constructive, and comprehensive reviews of our manuscript. Their valuable insights have significantly enhanced the methodological precision, theoretical depth, and clinical clarity of this paper. Below, we provide point-by-point responses to all comments alongside exact page and line references to the revised manuscript (clean version).

reviewer_points.comment: The authors should clarify how treatment fidelity was assessed across the 8 ACT intervention sessions.
reviewer_points.author_response: We thank Reviewer 1 for identifying this crucial methodological aspect. In the revised manuscript, we now explicitly detail that 20% of randomly selected audio-recorded therapy sessions were rated by two independent licensed clinical psychologists using the ACT Treatment Integrity Coding Manual. Inter-rater reliability was high (intraclass correlation coefficient = .89), confirming high fidelity to protocol.
reviewer_points.manuscript_action: Added comprehensive treatment fidelity protocol description in Section 2.3 (Intervention Protocol), Page 6, Lines 134–146.
reviewer_points.excerpt: "To verify treatment adherence, 20% of all audio-recorded intervention sessions were randomly selected and independently evaluated by two clinical psychologists using the ACT Treatment Integrity Coding Manual (intraclass correlation coefficient = .89). Fidelity ratings averaged 94.2% across sessions."

reviewer_points.comment: Please report Cohen's d or partial eta squared effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals for all primary outcome measures.
reviewer_points.author_response: We agree completely with this recommendation. In accordance with APA 7 and JCBS reporting standards, we have computed exact 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for all partial eta squared effect sizes in both the Results narrative and Table 2.
reviewer_points.manuscript_action: Updated Table 2 and Section 3.2 (Primary Outcomes), Page 9, Lines 201–215.
reviewer_points.excerpt: "Repeated-measures ANCOVA demonstrated a significant time-by-group interaction on pain disability (F(2, 57) = 14.82, p < .001, ηp² = 0.34, 95% CI [0.18, 0.48])."

reviewer_points.comment: The discussion should contrast the present results with recent findings by Hughes et al. (2023) regarding cognitive fusion trajectories in older versus younger pain cohorts.
reviewer_points.author_response: We appreciate this insightful suggestion. We have expanded our Discussion (Section 4.2) to integrate Hughes et al. (2023), specifically highlighting that age-related variations in experiential avoidance did not moderate defusion efficacy in our sample.
reviewer_points.manuscript_action: Expanded Discussion Section 4.2, Page 12, Paragraph 3, Lines 285–302.
reviewer_points.excerpt: "Consistent with recent evidence from Hughes et al. (2023), cognitive defusion operated as a robust mechanism across age strata, indicating that mindfulness-based experiential detachment does not depend on baseline pain chronicity or patient age."
